newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Recovery plays may tempt in weak SAfrica share mkt.
newsitem.headline: Recovery plays may tempt in weak SAfrica share mkt.

text.p: South African shares had a modest year in 1996 and this year is not tipped to be much better, but certain recovery and re-rated stocks will offer tempting opportunities, equity strategists said.
The market could be volatile given variables such as a rocky rand and the upcoming March 12 budget -- seen as a key test of the government's economic policy.

But most agreed that the year will see a basic pattern of a drifting first half, followed by a rise later in the year based on anticipation that 1998 will see a strengthening of the currently slowing South African economy.
"I think the market is going to be weak initially and then push up towards the end of the year as people look to 1998," said Andre Joubert, a portfolio manager at Investec.
The anticipated upturn should boost consumer confidence by the year-end and investors seeking to capitalise on that will head for stocks with a heavy retail exposure.

"Industrials and financial blue-chips with a consumer orientation should see a lot of interest later in the year," said Fleming Martin strategist Richard Jesse, citing stores group Wooltru and insurer Liberty Life as two possible gainers.
The stores sector also has recovery potential after a bad year in 1996 when it lost 24.88 percent of its value as companies posted a succession of poor results.

Old Mutual Unit Trusts portfolio manager Adrian Allardice said supermarket group Pick'n'Pay would also benefit from rejuvenated consumers. But he warned credit-dependent stores like Edgars and Foschini might do less well as banks kept a tight grip on customers' purse strings.

Strategists said 1996 had seen money ploughed into export-based rand-hedge stocks and this pattern might continue in the first half. But they added many investors would also want to punt cash into more risky cyclicals as the year draws on in a bid to catch 1998's anticipated upswing.
"The question is when do you shift from the rand-hedged stocks and go for the cyclicals?" said Tim Hacker, equity strategist at SBC Warburg.
One firm that many have tipped is pulp and paper group Sappi. It touched a year low of 39.25 rand last November, but a recovery may already be under way with the stock now at 46.20.

Some strategists said the steel sector also offered good recovery potential and tipped Highveld Steel as a possible bounce-back stock, as it is coming off a lower base than other major steel share Iscor.
But the shares will be risky. "The risk is very high and you really are betting on a turnaround in a commodity cycle. But they (steel shares) are coming off a low base," Joubert said.

Golds, bombed out by bullion's slump, are another area of uncertainty. "Golds are difficult to predict. The market is ignoring the rand-gold price and failing to guess the dollar-gold correctly. Everyone is looking for a floor in this (fall)," said Hacker.

Some said Goldfields of South Africa may outperform the sector if a long-mooted restructuring finally occurs. "There is so much value to be unlocked there, just the thought of a restructuring will drive the price up," said Joubert.

Elsewhere in mining, houses like Gencor, JCI and Anglovaal are seen as good solid investments. But strategists said the mining exploration sector -- which saw a 1996 gain of nearly 100 percent and was the JSE's best performing sector -- might again offer high returns to more speculative-minded investors.

Electronics looks to be a more mixed sector this year with strategists seeing general firms like Plessey hampered by their exposure to low levels of new line installation from state telecommunications provider Telkom.

But firms exposed to information technology are set to build on their boom in 1996, which boosted the electronics index nearly 40 percent and made it the JSE's sixth best performer. Demand in the industry is still high and firms are expected to use strong balance sheets to fund buying sprees.
DiData and Q Data were both tipped.
Most strategists also saw the construction sector doing well from a low base after a dismal 1996 when it lost 35.30 percent of its value and was the JSE's worst performing index.

Strategists expect an upsurge in government infrastructure projects in 1997 to kick-start the industry. Major shares like Murray & Roberts, Group Five and Stocks & Stocks could all post gains, they said.
